speechtext:
I just quoted right from the book. If the minister wants to change the law books, that is fine with me.
Let me contrast that statement with the words of Mr. Justice Brandeis, one of the most fair minded judges who has ever graced the bench of the Supreme Court of the United States. In his famous dissent in the case of Olmstead versus the United States he said:
Decency, security and liberty alike demand that government officials shall be subjected to the same rules of conduct that are commands to the citizen. In a government of laws, existence of the government will be imperiled if it fails to observe the law scrupulously. Our government is the potent, the omnipresent teacher. For good or ill, it teaches the whole people by its example. Crime is contagious. If the government becomes a lawbreaker, it breeds contempt for law; it invites every man to become a law unto himself, it invites anarchy. To declare that in the administration of the criminal law, the end justifies the means-to declare that the government may commit crimes in order to secure the conviction of a private criminal-would bring terrible retribution. Against that pernicious doctrine this Court should resolutely set its face.
In other words, I do not think evidence illegally obtained should be admitted, because if you allow the police to break the law they will do so.
I do not mean to suggest by referring to an American decision that I am advocating the strict exclusionary doctrine that has developed in that country. In the United States, generally speaking, evidence is not admissible in a court of law that is illegally obtained. The application of this strict rule has led to scandalous abuse. There must be a balance, and I should like to see that balance in our jurisprudence.
Nevertheless, there is a large constituency in and out of our profession which adheres to the belief that the Ontario court of appeal in the Wray case was right-that Privy Council decisions touching the same concerns were right-that Their Lordships Cartwright, Spence and Hall, dissenting in Wray, were right, and that the court must consider factors other than just

May 11, 1977
Criminal Code
relevancy. I quote Mr. Justice Spence, in his dissenting judgment, who said:
I am most strongly of the opinion that it is the duty of every judge to guard against bringing the administration of justice into disrepute. That is a duty which lies upon him constantly and that is a duty which he must always keep firmly in mind. The proper discharge of this duty is one which, in the present day of almost riotous disregard for the administration of justice, is of paramount importance to the continued life of the state.
Unfortunately, few Canadians are aware of the serious ramifications flowing from the Supreme Court decision in the Wray case.
That prospect is frightening enough, but perhaps the most disheartening aspect of the Wray case is that the court's decision has the unintended effect of giving judicial permission to participation by the state in the illegal conduct of policemen. The rule in Wray denies any value other than the search for truth. But I quote Viscount Knight Bruce, who said:
... truth, like all the good things, may be loved unwisely, may be pursued too keenly-may cost too much.
But since the Wray case was decided in 1970, neither parliament nor the courts have taken any action to reverse the dangerous precedent that was set, despite the sensible guidelines regarding judicial discretion which have been issued by the Law Reform Commission of Canada.
Indeed, not only has Wray remained as the law of the land, but since 1970 the Supreme Court's ruling has obviously assumed the proportions of a huge umbrella under the shelter of which many of Canada's prosecutors feel impelled to tender as evidence some very questionable items, and the courts are required to condone practices that prior to the Wray case would have been totally unacceptable.
I want to refer now to what has been going on, Mr. Speaker. According to the annual report of the Governor General as it pertains to wiretapping, for the period of 1976-77, 548 authorizations were given under Section 423 of the Criminal Code; 21 authorizations under Section 192 of the Customs Act; 529 authorizations under the Narcotic Control Act; 106 under the Food and Drugs Act; 11 under Section 163 of the Excise Act, and one under 158 of the Excise Act.
Perhaps the most interesting statistic in the report shows that 1,062 persons were arrested whose identity became known to a peace officer as a result of an interception under an authorization. The number of criminal proceedings commenced at the instance of the Attorney General of Canada in which private communications obtained by interception under an authorization were adduced in evidence and the number of such proceedings that resulted in a conviction was 13. That is, criminal proceedings, 13; convictions 13.
I do not know what to think about this, Mr. Speaker. We see that when we give the police too much authority it results in 1,062 arrests.
Now I will turn to something that the minister spent most of his time on, gun control. Many of the amendments we suggested to the House in debate proved true and have been incorporated in the bill. I am thankful for that. It is like a prayer, Mr. Speaker-I am thankful for what I am about to receive. I am

happy to say that we have helped bury Bill C-83. The function of the opposition was fulfilled in this case-with excellence.

That reminds me of the man who in 1975 raped six women but in 1976 only raped three, so he contended he was better. This means that Canadians did not know about 2,673 orders. A former Prime Minister said one should know the law, and as the minister well knows, ignorance of the law is no defence. Mr. Speaker, as the minister knows, the committee considering Bill C-83 won a battle.

The duties of the commissioner are substantial. He will be busy indeed, being responsible for the issuing of permits, dealing with prohibited and restricted weapons and issuing certificates to people who want to buy guns. I now deal with the clause which I think it is good to include in the bill and which I hope will do the necessary job. I am speaking of the clause relating to dangerous offenders. In March this year I addressed a question to the Minister of Justice concerning an inmate of an institution who had been released on mandatory parole by right of law. That person had, on several occasions, been charged with raping children aged six and seven. He applied to be released on parole. The Saskatoon parole division was not empowered by law to refuse that parole. The chairman of the Saskatoon parole division wrote a letter to the Calgary parole division about this man who had raped children. This man has lived a life of crime, involving rape and indecent assault, and it was feared that he was capable of killing his next victim. Unfortunately, this man was released in society. He left Saskatoon and came to Calgary, where he was an unwelcome guest.
I have put before the House our position on this bill and have said where we stand on the question of electronic surveillance, or bugging. As I tried to explain carefully, and I argued by referring to case law and precedents, judicial interpretation of electronic surveillance provisions has placed too much power in the hands of those in authority. I tried to show how such power can be abused, to the detriment of the citizens of Canada. We must examine this question as well in committee.
I spoke of the difficulties associated with gun control rules and regulations, and mentioned some of the weaknesses and strengths of the bill. I was greatly impressed with the erudition of the hon. member for Calgary North and listened with interest to his arguments concerning the wiretap provisions of the bill, arguments he backed with case law. It is refreshing to hear an argument backed with that kind of in-depth research and logic. Too often we deal with such questions on the basis of emotionalism rather than logic. When speaking of wiretapping the hon. member did himself and his party and, indeed, the entire opposition, proud. Later I shall speak in some detail on gun control but for a moment let me deal with wire-tapping.
First let me say that in my remarks I do not intend to reflect on the ruling Mr. Speaker handed down in this House relating to the procedural point which we raised several days ago. Unfortunately our present procedures, which follow parliamentary tradition, do not give members of this House any chance on second reading to distinguish between their support or otherwise of wiretapping and gun control. That procedure is unfortunate, and it seems to me a device must be found beyond that suggested by the Speaker, which simply involves deletion on third reading. We need desperately a proceeding which will apply to the second reading vote, which is most important, in order to enable the public to understand our positions.
Obviously, in terms of gun control, this is a compromise bill. We have half a loaf, which is sometimes better than no loaf at all. But we do not support the wiretap provisions of the bill. We feel as strongly and vigorously as we ever felt that those provisions of the bill are an insidious invasion of the privacy of Canadians. These further extensions of that insidious invasion must be resisted by members of the opposition in the interests of their constituents and in the interests of freedom of the mind, that freedom of the mind which all Canadians cherish.
Why I say that the whole wiretap question becomes one that is insidious and, in a sense, immoral is that in the mind of a

May 11, 1977
Criminal Code
citizen, he must believe he is free. Surely that is one of the things that distinguishes Canada from totalitarian countries. However, you cannot feel you are free if you think you are tapped. You cannot feel free if you do not know whether there is a bug on your telephone. The wiretap amendments that have come down have expanded, not reduced, the areas of the law where wiretap becomes available.
I want to deal very briefly with the report of 1976 to the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) on the operations of the wiretap law. My understanding is that this does not deal with the many, many wiretaps that go out in terms of provincial attorneys general. These are the wiretaps that have gone out under federal statute only. I do not have the figures for the whole country in terms of province by province, just those that went out by federal statute.
In 1976, 1,224 telephones were tapped. That led to 1,062 arrests, but proceedings against 368 individuals. Of the 1,062 arrested, there were 824 whose names did not appear on the request for authorization. That means they were fishing expeditions. Innocent citizens were subjected to taps on fishing expeditions. That is surely something that we who cherish freedom in this country should oppose.
In 1976, 517 warrants were granted under the Official Secrets Act. The average time of each of those warrants was 241 days. All 614 original applications for wiretapping were granted. There was not a single denial by a judge, yet we have had the police, the law enforcement agencies, lobbying the minister over and over that they should not need to have their requests reviewed before a judge. Here the judiciary has clearly co-operated with law enforcement by turning down none. Only two of the 614 applications had any limitation at all in the terms and conditions attached to those wiretap approvals.
Nine warrants allowed police officers to listen for more than 180 days. What we have had is a rubber stamp provision under the wiretap law.
The minister raised the question of the good feeling in the committee that in fact the provisions for notification have now been reduced from the suggested five years to three years. I agree that consensus was developed around that. However, that argument about a consensus was a nice little carrot that the minister hung in front of the committee.
The key to the wiretap bill is the expansion of the offences. That is the insidious part. Let me give an example of what could happen under the wiretap provisions as they are now proposed.
Clause 7(1) (c) states that an offence mentioned in section 192 of the Customs Act (smuggling) is a wiretap offence. I ask hon. members how many people in their constituencies have ever come across the border with an extra can of beer or a pair of pants under their ordinary pants. Smuggling in Canada has become very widespread. It is a kind of human failing. Let us be realistic about the question of smuggling. A lot of people may take an extra package of cigarettes across the border. A tap can be made for that offence. No judge can deny the

authorization to issue the tap. It is a case of "open sesame" to tap ever body the police wish.
Under the offence sections, comprising the guts of the wiretap provisions, it is so broad that there is almost nothing for which the police cannot tap. That is why we in this House must resist to the best of our ability this insidious invasion of the rights of individuals and, more important, the right of Canadians to feel they are free in their own minds so that they can pick up their telephone and have a conversation without thinking they have to be guarded in what they say. We know that happens in countries in eastern Europe and so on, but surely in the kind of democracy we have developed on the North American continent and to a large extent under British and Western European tradition, we should continue to protect the rights of people to feel free in their own minds.
There are other provisions in the wiretap section to which we take exception. The hon. member for Calgary North referred to them. There is no reason why police should be rewarded for illegal conduct. We should support our police in every way. They have a difficult job. However, when they cut a corner, when they do not bother with an authorization from a judge, when they go out on a job with the impression that it is O.K. because it is pretty important that they catch a particular person-I agree that it is important to catch a criminal-that little review process of going to a judge is very important in order to avoid abuses.
As a result of a breach of the wiretap provisions the police obtain illegal evidence. The tape is not admitted in court, but everything they learn from the tape goes into evidence. If that is the case, there will be a law for the police and a law for other people, because they can introduce illegal evidence as a result of illegal activity, but the rest of the population must abide by the law.
That is an unsound principle in our law. I am disappointed that the minister has not yet seen fit to accept what is now common practice in the United States. He has not accepted something that the British Bar Association has looked at very seriously and may very well accept. Instead, he has accepted the hoary old argument that if it is any kind of evidence, no matter where it is from, throw it all in. That reduces the standard of police work.
It is very easy to sit at one end of electronic equipment and listen to people. However, it can be seen from the records introduced by the hon. member for Calgary North and myself that the amount of convictions obtained in that way is almost nil. It is peanuts.
The police should be getting out from behind their earphones on to the street getting good, hard evidence the way policemen always did, through meeting and talking to people and getting informants.
When Ramsey Clark was the attorney general of the United States, he had the best record for getting Mafia convictions. He refused to use wiretapping. Instead of wasting police time, he told the police to get back out on to the streets to see what was happening. He told them not to waste their time listening
May 11, 1977

to bedroom conversations, something that was quite common in the United States under their law.
The offensive part of this legislation is clearly the wiretap provisions. I am very disappointed that we keep getting this hoary old thing thrown back at us in an omnibus bill, confusing the issue of gun control with wiretapping.
Under the gun control provisions, I said earlier that half a loaf is better than no bread at all.

You guys have the apples, we eat the bread. In any event, there is obviously a little food in it for all of us.
Under the gun control provisions, we should not proceed further in this debate without saying something about those individuals who fought very hard for the safety of Canadians in terms of gun control legislation. I am thinking particularly of Mr. and Mrs. Slinger whose son died during a very tragic event in Brampton. But they did not sit back and wring their hands. They decided to go to work to protect other people in Canada, to protect other sons.
I think of Maggie Burtinshaw of British Columbia who faced a severe personal tragedy when her son died. She did not sit back and wring her hands. She went out and did as a good citizen should. She went out and worked for a change in the law. Now, this change in the law may not go as far as Maggie Burtinshaw and others may wish, but I have to admit that it does go a significant distance toward curing what has been a major fault under our criminal law, that is, failure to reduce what we can call preventable homicide in cases where you can predict the behaviour of an individual who is unable to control his own emotions. The measure before us does provide a review process by requiring him to obtain a firearms certificate.
Sometimes statistics are dry,- but on this occasion they tell an interesting story. Forty-six percent of all murders committed in Canada are domestic murders. The gun control lobbyists always maintain that you will never take the guns away from the criminals. But a criminal is not a guy who runs around the streets with a big "C" on his forehead so that he can be identified. There are a lot of criminals who are first offenders-they were not criminals until they committed an offence. And they are people just like you and me who have lost control of themselves. Those people are certainly involved in 46 per cent of the domestic homicides in Canada. In some 44 per cent of those cases the agent of death is a firearm, and 72 per cent of those firearms are rifles. These are hard statistics which we cannot avoid considering carefully.
The last statistic of importance is one which shows that in the United States 54 per cent of the homicides involve the use of the handgun, not the rifle. Almost the reverse situation occurs in Canada. In this country in only 10.4 per cent of cases is the agent of death a handgun. Therefore the gun control system we have used in Canada to date in terms of handguns
Criminal Code
has, in my view, significantly reduced the number of Canadian homicides in the area of handguns.

The percentage of homicides where the handgun is used as the agent of death in the United States is 54 per cent, and in Canada it is only 10.4 per cent. In Canada we have a very strict handgun law and in the United States they have very poor handgun laws.
My argument is that gun control provisions, contrary to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Calgary North, do have a significant effect on reducing homicide right across the country. That is the reason I welcome this half loaf which is presented in terms of a firearms bill, and I think the hon. member for Calgary North may also welcome it, even if for different reasons.
When we get to the positive aspects of the measure before us I would agree that the efforts made by the hon. member for Calgary North and others in the committee to take away the guarantor provision were a positive step. Eliminating it did, in fact, reduce an unnecessary elitism in the system by which you had to know somebody important in order to get a licence. I agree it was desirable to remove that proposal.
Establishing the cost of the firearms certificate at $2 per year is something about which nobody can reasonably complain. Specific examples of preventable homicide are numerous. I shall not bore the House with many of them. These are headlines: October 23, 1976, "Bought Gun for Protection; Man Shoots Son by Mistake." "Lethbridge-Boy's Purchase of Rifle Leads to Homicide." September 12, 1974, "Children Watched as Mother Gunned Down by Commonlaw Husband." These were preventable homicides. They were cases where the conduct of the murderer was predictable because he had previously indicated the presence of mental disorder, or had a record of previous criminal activity. In those kinds of homicides the provisions contained in the bill are significant.
But what the bill fails to deal with is the six million rifles which are still out there in the hands of a few unstable people-a very minor percentage. One of the things we will get to, because of the provisions of the bill, in about 50 years is the reduction of the proliferation of firearms. Under the provisions of the bill you cannot transfer a rifle and you cannot sell your rifle unless the person you are transferring it to has a firearms certificate. Therefore the effect of these provisions will be to bring the licensing system to bear, and ultimately there will be a reduction in the number of emotionally unstable individuals who have access to firearms.
Competency training is useful but it does not provide an emotional test. In fact training someone to shoot straight may lead to a murder rather than to a wounding. Competency training is no answer to the question of gun control. However, I do not intend to criticize competency training. I think it is useful that a person know how to handle his weapons, and it should certainly reduce the number of negligent homicides which could occur during a foray into the forest.

I do, however, wish to deal with a key weakness in the bill which deserves examination when the measure goes to committee. I am referring to the provision dealing with mental disorders. We are in a position of risking a computer bank which will have information about everybody in the country in terms of where they were treated and what happened to them mentally. That is something to which I object as strenuously as I object to the wiretapping provisions. We do not want Big Brother to fill that computer full of information about private mental histories of people in Canada.
I urge the minister to be sure that when the applications for the firearms certificates are made up there is a question concerning whether the applicant has been treated for a mental disorder. Second, if the answer is yes, there must be a question concerning where and by whom the applicant was treated. Last, there must be a consent form in the application so that the firearms licensing officer has a full opportunity to investigate the information contained on the application. I do not know what the minister has in mind, but if the purpose of that section is to put mental hospital computer data in the possession of those not otherwise authorized to receive it, then 1 object to that practice as strenuously as I did to electronic invasion of privacy. It is another serious invasion of the right of Canadians to privacy. But I will say this: when a person applies for a firearms permit he is asking not for a right but for a privilege, and should consent to a search of the records being undertaken so that whoever issues a licence may know it is not being given to an unsuitable person. I agree with this in principle, although how it will work out in practice is, to say the least, uncertain.
The minister referred to a Gallup poll dealing with the way Canadians feel about gun control. He pointed out, I think, that 85 per cent were in favour of some form of gun control measures. What he did not tell us was that this 85 per cent approved Bill C-83 and the principles underlying it. In fact, that 85 per cent was not answering a question about new purchasers of weapons; it was answering a question about registration in terms of the whole ballgame.

Mr. Speaker, in beginning my speech this afternoon there are some observations I would like to make with respect to this bill, and the subject matter of this bill, which has had such a checkered career in this parliament.
In view of what the legislation says with respect to firearms control, I am greatly surprised by the fact the minister devoted so much time, out of the time allotted to him, in the course of his speech to that particular provision in the bill. As the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wooliiams) said, there was a tremendous parliamentary battle fought over that earlier.
I want to join with the hon. member for Calgary North in supporting the purpose of the amendment which he has put. I think it is a wrong parliamentary practice. I argued the case on a point of order the other night in another matter. We place in the legislation that comes before us so many sections dealing with different aspects that, as the hon. member for New Westminister (Mr. Leggatt) said the other evening, one may feel that he or she should vote nay to the entire bill. One may feel that he or she should vote nay because there is a difficulty with a group of sections, and yet be bound to vote yea, or be perceived to vote yea.
It is a blot on our legislative process that we have come to a point where that procedure is acceptable. It has been upheld by the Speaker on the basis of precedent that various aspects of a subject matter, or even unrelated subject matters, or even subject matters with respect to different statutes, can be dealt with in the same bill. The result of all of this is that it makes it difficult for members of parliament to be accountable. By the votes they cast, I believe it tends to prolong parliamentary debate that must follow, because members of parliament feel they must explain themselves with respect to their votes on account of the difficulties of misconstruction-

What I was saying was that it was unfortunate that the Chair was bound by precedent, a precedent in a matter which makes it difficult, on the one hand, for the public to understand, and on the other hand for parliamentarians to explain their actions in terms of votes and accounting for those votes.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, an observation of that nature is not a reflection on the Chair; it is a reflection on an unfortunate precedent which the Chair must follow in these circumstances. I take second place to no member of the House in regard to the respect which I show the Chair. I have to confess that from time to time I disagree with decisions of the Chair, but I am as aware as anyone of the position the Chair is in under our rules, the fact that there is no appeal from its rulings. This places a great responsibility on the Chair, and because of this my respect for the Chair is increased. I think it does not advance the debate in any way for the Postmaster General to rise in his place and show what is in fact a bona fide disrespect for the Chair by intervening the way he did, by asking the Chair to intervene by raising a spurious point of order.
Perhaps because of our complex legislative process or because we tend in modern society today to intervene to a greater and greater extent in the lives of individuals, this parliament is busier than ever, which means it is necessary for more and more provisions to be packed into fewer and fewer bills. That may be the case, or there may be a thousand explanations. It may be, as the deputy opposition whip said, a matter of some cunning on the part of the government, which I suspect might be the case. But whatever the reason, it is unfortunate that this is deemed to be acceptable parliamentary practice.

it because it does not really affect us at all. It does affect us, it affects us very badly, and on reflection I think that when the people of Canada view this bill and consider it in terms of the use of the new devices of electronic surveillance, the extension of the use, the lack of notice, and the power that is given to the police in an extended way, they will be asking the government some questions. There is a duty on the government to explain why it asks this parliament to extend those powers.
I hope there will be some speakers on the government side who will, for once, not sit mute and not acquiesce in whatever the minister says is all right, who will rise in their places and, on the basis of some evidence that they can present to the House during the course of this debate, tell us what has happened in the country that we have to place in the hands of the police, however well intentioned they may be, the power to intrude on our civil rights. I hope they will tell us why it has been necessary to take cognizance of the cases that were brought forward by the hon. member for Calgary North. The
Criminal Code
hon. member indicated that if the law is not followed-the law that this parliament dealt with-then the evidence that has been procured as a result of the law not being followed is still admitted in a court of law.
I think parliament has to take a look at that kind of question that has not been answered. I think the hon. member for Calgary North has done the House and the people of the country a great service by putting on the record the number of cases that have come to his attention and are likely to continue unless we, in the course of the discussions on this bill, review it carefully and decide whether or not circumstances have deteriorated to the extent that police should have these powers. My suggestion is that they cannot.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
